extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent examiners, patent attorneys, and judges (U.S. patent context)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for whether a claimed subject is patentable under 18th–19th century U.S. patent statutes as explained in judicial decision: what counts as an invention vs. a mere discovery, novelty/priority, disclosure requirements, and limits on the Commissioner’s duty to issue a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (must contrive/produce what did not exist before)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must invent, contrive, or produce something that did not exist before; the patent must be founded upon an invention or the invention of a new improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Cranch: "The applicant must invent, contrive, or produce something that did not exist before." Examples/explanation: placing ice blocks on edge is not an invention because the act of placing them that way existed before; a mere existing act is not a new contrivance. Patents are justified only by this act of creation, not by mere recognition of pre-existing things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discovery of a pre-existing fact is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a new effect of something which existed before (a 'mere naked discovery') is not the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual examples: the discovery that "ice so placed keeps longer" is a fact that 'existed before' and therefore cannot alone justify a patent. The decision repeatedly states that discovering a beneficial effect of an old means does not constitute an invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory wording treats 'discovery' as synonymous with 'invention' for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'discover' and 'invent' differ in common usage, under the Constitution and patent statutes the terms are used synonymously to require something equivalent to invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge draws on legislative history and statutory sections (1790, 1793, 1836, 1839 acts) to show the statutes contemplate discovery only insofar as it amounts to invention — i.e., "discovery" in the statutes means discovery of something new (equivalent to invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter: 'new and useful' art, invention, or improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may issue only for some 'new and useful art, discovery, invention, or improvement' (per the cited sections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical requirements following from this principle: the claimed subject must be new, useful, and properly the subject of a patent under the statutes; the Commissioner must consider whether the thing claimed is a 'new' art or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description, drawings, model, signature, and oath requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Before receiving a patent, the inventor must deliver a written description of the invention, with drawings and (where applicable) a model, signed by the inventor, and make oath that he believes he is the original and first inventor (statutory requisites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge notes the statutes require a written description "by which it may be distinguished from other inventions," drawings, model, signature, and oath. These formalities are part of obtaining a patent but do not substitute for patentable inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / full, clear, and exact description to enable skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and the manner of making, constructing, and using it in "such full, clear and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art" to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge emphasizes the enabling function of the specification as the statutory test for sufficiency of disclosure; model/drawings and a full specification suffice even if the invention has not been put into actual public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's duty under 7th section: examine novelty and issue patent if not shown prior
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner must examine the alleged new invention and, if it does not appear to the Commissioner that it had been invented or discovered by any other person in this country prior thereto, or patented, or described in print, or in public use/on sale with the applicant's consent prior to application, and if he deems it sufficiently useful and important, he shall issue a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge quotes the 7th section as creating a prima facie duty to issue a patent when statutory disqualifications are not shown. The Commissioner’s examination focuses on prior invention, prior patent/publication, and public use/sale with consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner may refuse patent even when 7th-section objections absent (not within patentable subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the specific objections enumerated in the 7th section are not present, the Commissioner must still decide whether the invention is new and whether it is the proper subject of a patent and may refuse if it is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge explains that the Commissioner is not limited to the narrow list in the 7th section; he must refuse patents that are not genuinely inventions (e.g., mere discoveries) even if no prior patent/publication/use is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: New means/contrivance required to apply a discovered effect
rubrics_metrics.description: If the thing discovered is a beneficial effect, the application of that discovery is patentable only if it employs new means, a contrivance, or production of something that did not before exist; old means producing a new effect do not justify a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the ice case: the beneficial effect (retarding dissolution) was discovered, but no new means are proposed — hence ineligible. Prior cases (Tudor, Dollond) are discussed where the office considered whether the means used were new inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calling an act a 'system' or 'plan' does not make it patentable if the act itself is old
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling the claim as a 'system' or 'plan' (including intent or purpose) cannot supply novelty if the underlying act is not new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge notes that a 'system' requires a combination of many things acting together; simply asserting intent or purpose with an old act does not create an invention. The ice claim asked only for "placing the prepared blocks edgewise," not a true system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice (actual use) is not required to obtain a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes do not require that an invention be put into public use or reduced to actual practice before a patent is issued, except as concerns certain statutory provisions on prior use or forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge contrasts U.S. law with English practice and explains models/drawings/specifications are sufficient. He rejects the argument that the first inventor must have reduced the invention to practice to obtain the patent; courts ultimately decide validity if contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay/non-use and 'abandonment' can defeat patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-use may lead to forfeiture only when it amounts to abandonment; the statutes provide that failure to put the invention on sale for eighteen months may be relevant, and abandonment is a jury question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge cites the 18-month sale requirement as an exception and discusses the act of March 3, 1839, section 7, which protects certain prior uses by others. Abandonment to the public can be a statutory bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent granted to later inventor prior to earlier inventor’s application does not automatically bar the first inventor (priority/interference rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent issued to a second inventor prior to the first inventor's application is not necessarily a bar to a patent to the first inventor; the Commissioner has jurisdiction to decide priority in interference cases under the 8th section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge explains statutory scheme: Congress gave the Commissioner authority to decide priority and grant patents in interference situations; rights do not depend on whether a subsequent inventor had put the thing into practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant may show plaintiff's specification omits truth or that patentee was not original inventor (15th-section defenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: In infringement suits the defendant may offer evidence that the plaintiff's specification does not contain the whole truth about the invention, or that the patentee was not the original and first inventor of the thing patented or a substantial part thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge cites the 15th section which enumerates matters admissible in evidence under the general issue, including proof that the patentee wasn't the original inventor or that the specification is false or incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent invalid if patentee claims more than he had right to claim; Commissioner may reissue corrected patent (13th-section)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent is invalid because the patentee claimed more than he had a right to claim as new, the Commissioner may cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the same invention with proper scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge references the 13th section allowing correction (reissue) where an overbroad claim was made; the statute contemplates limiting claims to what is truly new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are monopolies and should be strictly confined to what natural right of property justifies
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent is a monopoly and, except for the natural right of property in one's labor and ingenuity, it is in derogation of common right and should therefore be strictly confined to the case excepted (i.e., genuine inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge uses this principle to justify strict construction of patent claims and to refuse patents for mere discoveries or obvious acts. It is used as a policy touchstone for deciding borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent/publication/public use/on-sale with consent bars issuance under statutory test
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is disqualified if prior to the applicant's invention it had been patented or described in printed publication in any country, or had been in public use or on sale with the applicant's consent or allowance prior to application (as enumerated in the 7th section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge quotes the 7th section conditions and explains the Commissioner must examine these grounds; the timing nuance (prior to invention vs prior to application) is discussed in statutory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'rule' to grant patents in doubtful cases is no longer controlling once remedies exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical office rule that where the question is doubtful the patent should be granted arose when applicants lacked remedies; after statutory remedies (e.g., equity bills) exist, that rule loses force and the Commissioner need not grant in doubtful cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge explains that because applicants may now seek equity if refused, the prior administrative policy of granting doubtful cases is no longer a binding reason to issue patents that appear not to be inventions.
